# Fall River/New Bedford Line

The Fall River/New Bedford Line is a commuter rail line operated by the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) in southeastern Massachusetts, United States. Formerly known as the Middleborough/Lakeville Line, it was renamed following the extension of service to Fall River and New Bedford on March 24, 2025 . The line connects these South Coast cities to Boston's South Station for the first time in over 65 years, after passenger service was discontinued in 1958 .

## 1. History

### 1.1 Original Service and Closure

The history of rail service to Fall River and New Bedford dates back to the 19th century. The Old Colony and Fall River Railroad Company was formed on June 20, 1854, through the merger of the Old Colony Railroad and the Fall River Railroad, creating a two-pronged line from Boston to Plymouth and Boston to Fall River, splitting at South Braintree . The company later expanded to include service to New Bedford.

For nearly a century, the New Haven Railroad operated the South Coast train route . However, declining ridership led to the closure of passenger service in 1958 . New Bedford had a rail connection to Boston for the first time since 1958 when service resumed in 2025 .

### 1.2 South Coast Rail Project Development

The South Coast Rail project was first proposed in the 1980s with the intent of bringing economic development to the Fall River and New Bedford areas . New Bedford and Fall River peaked economically in the 1940s and declined significantly in the 1970s .

The project faced numerous challenges and delays over several decades. In April 2007, Governor Deval Patrick released "South Coast Rail: A Plan for Action," detailing the steps that would be taken to bring commuter rail to Fall River and New Bedford. Patrick said the project's estimated price tag was \$1 billion .

The project had many stops and starts as officials gathered funding and deliberated over possible routes . The most recent groundbreaking took place in 2019, after the state settled on a plan to connect South Coast cities to the existing Middleborough/Lakeville line, avoiding a more difficult and expensive option to build tracks through the Hockomock Swamp toward the Stoughton line .

### 1.3 Construction and Opening

Early Action construction projects began in 2019 to prepare for the larger Phase 1 main line rail construction contracts . The first visible active construction projects were drainage culvert replacement and a major railroad grade crossing update in New Bedford. This work also included the construction of 5 wetland mitigation areas in the corridor and was substantially completed in Summer 2020 .

The Fall River Secondary Line Construction contract was awarded to Skanska DW White JV on May 11, 2020 . Work on the Fall River Secondary included track, stations, bridges, and a layover facility. Construction began in summer 2020 and was completed in time for the March 24, 2025 opening .

The long-awaited project cost the MBTA more than \$1 billion to construct . On March 24, 2025, the Middleborough/Lakeville Line was officially renamed the Fall River/New Bedford Line as service was extended to Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, and Fall River .

## 2. Service Description

### 2.1 Route and Stations

The Fall River/New Bedford Line operates with two branches that converge at East Taunton Station. The line runs from Boston's South Station through Middleborough and East Taunton to one of two branches: one continuing to Fall River and the other to New Bedford .

The line serves a total of 15 stations, including six new stations constructed as part of the extension . The stations are:

**Boston Branch (existing stations)**:

* South Station

* JFK/UMass

* Quincy Center

* Braintree

* Holbrook/Randolph

* Montello

* Brockton

* Campello

* Bridgewater

* Middleborough

**New Bedford Branch (new stations)**:

* East Taunton

* Freetown

* Church Street (New Bedford)

* New Bedford

**Fall River Branch (new stations)**:

* East Taunton

* Freetown

* Fall River Depot

The New Bedford Branch has two stations in New Bedford: one near downtown (New Bedford Station at 536 Acushnet Avenue) and another on Church Street in the North End (Church Street Station at 387 Church Street) .

### 2.2 Service Frequency and Schedule

The MBTA operates 32 daily weekday trips between Boston and the South Coast on the new line . There are 15 weekday trips on the Fall River Line and 17 trips on the New Bedford Line .

Weekday direct service runs approximately every 70 minutes . Inbound trains from New Bedford Station run from 4:27 a.m. to 9:23 p.m., with 14 total departing trains throughout the day. Outbound trains from South Station have weekday departures from 6:45 a.m. to 11:59 p.m. .

On weekends, the Fall River/New Bedford Line operates 26 trips between South Station and the South Coast . Weekend direct service runs approximately every 120 minutes . Inbound trains on weekends leave New Bedford Station from 4:47 a.m. to 9:53 p.m., with seven departures throughout the day. Outbound trains leave South Station from 6:37 a.m. to 11:59 p.m. .

### 2.3 Travel Times

Direct rides from downtown New Bedford to Boston's South Station take about 94 to 98 minutes . Some trips that require a transfer in East Taunton take about two hours . The scheduled trip time from Fall River and New Bedford to Boston is roughly 90 minutes, which is generally faster than car travel during rush hour .

The first train is scheduled to leave New Bedford Station at 4:27 a.m., stopping at Church Street Station at 4:33 a.m. and arriving at Boston's South Station at 6:01 a.m. .

## 3. Infrastructure and Equipment

### 3.1 Track and Right-of-Way

Phase 1 of the South Coast Rail project reconstructs 12.1 miles of the Fall River Secondary and 24.1 miles of Middleborough Secondary and the New Bedford Main Line . The project uses the Middleborough Secondary (currently a freight line) to provide service to Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River. The Middleborough Secondary connects to Cotley Junction in East Taunton .

From Cotley Junction, Phase 1 trains join the New Bedford Main Line and continue to New Bedford, or they branch off on the Fall River Secondary to Fall River (this area is known as the Southern Triangle) .

### 3.2 Rolling Stock

The MBTA uses EMD F40PH diesel-electric locomotives on the Fall River/New Bedford Line . The F40PH is a 4-axle B-B locomotive with 3,000-3,200 horsepower (2.2-2.4 MW) built by the Electro-Motive Division of General Motors between 1975 and 1992 .

For passenger cars, the MBTA ordered 80 bilevel cars to provide immediate relief for the retirement of the MBB cars and for the completion of the South Coast Rail project. The extension to Fall River and New Bedford alone required 16 new bilevel cars, the first of which arrived on MBTA property in late 2022 .

### 3.3 Stations

All stations on the Fall River/New Bedford Line comply with MBTA standards and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements, which include high-level platforms for "all-doors" boarding . Other amenities include benches, canopies, bicycle storage, and parking facilities.

The new stations feature modern designs with accessible platforms, lighting, and passenger information systems. Parking is available at many stations, with standard rates of $4 per day on weekdays and $2 per day on weekends/holidays .

## 4. Operations

### 4.1 Fare Structure

The standard one-way fare for a trip from the South Coast stations to South Station is $12.25. Reduced fare is $6 for riders who qualify . Standard monthly passes are $388, and reduced monthly passes are $190 .

Children aged 11 and younger do not need a ticket . Unlimited weekend passes are available for \$10 .

### 4.2 Ticketing

Riders can buy tickets on the MBTA's mTicket app, or with cash or card onboard the train . For more information on buying tickets, the MBTA provides detailed guides on their website.

### 4.3 Parking

Parking is available at most stations on the Fall River/New Bedford Line. During the promotional period following the line's opening, parking was free at six stations from March 24 until the end of day on April 30, 2025: Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Church Street, Fall River Depot, and New Bedford .

After the promotional period, standard parking rates apply: $4 per day on weekdays and $2 per day on weekends/holidays . Overnight parking is allowed at most stations, but at New Bedford Station it comes with a multi-day rate of \$15 per day .

Parking can be paid for using the PayByPhone app at most MBTA lots .

## 5. Economic Impact and Development

### 5.1 Tourism and Visitor Impact

The Fall River/New Bedford Line has had a significant impact on tourism in the South Coast region. At the New Bedford Whaling Museum, ticket sales are up 30% compared to the previous year, largely driven by Boston-area visitors. President and CEO Amanda McMullen says the train is the only explanation for the sudden spike .

The extra admission revenue is helping to fund museum initiatives that are hard to find grants for, including upgrades to the ticket system and computer servers that support the museum's digital catalog .

The Whaling Museum has stepped up its advertising, using geographically targeted social media posts and video ad buys in Boston's South Station, the northernmost point on the Fall River/New Bedford Line .

### 5.2 Economic Development and Housing

South Coast Rail is anticipated to offer significant economic and housing development, as well as educational and recreational opportunities throughout southeastern Massachusetts with area residents having much easier access to the many amenities of the South Coast and connections to downtown Boston .

Boosting economic growth through increased access to Boston is expected to attract businesses, create jobs, and expand housing opportunities . The line is also expanding educational access, with more students from greater Boston and surrounding areas able to easily commute to UMass Dartmouth, enhancing diversity and enrollment .

New Bedford's new "transit-oriented development" zoning districts are designed to encourage development near the train stations . A hotel to be built near New Bedford Station was approved, and developers are showing increased interest in building housing near the stations .

### 5.3 Ridership Growth

The Fall River/New Bedford Line has experienced significant ridership growth. On average, riders are taking 2,000 more trips each day compared to pre-extension levels . Weekday ridership increased by 36%, while weekend ridership increased by 13% .

Commuting workers, rather than leisure travelers, appear to make up most of the increased ridership . This suggests the line is fulfilling its primary purpose of connecting South Coast residents to employment opportunities in Boston and other areas along the route.

## 6. Future Plans

### 6.1 Full Build Phase (Phase 2)

The South Coast Rail project has a second phase, known as the "Full Build" . Phase 2 would turn the South Coast lines into an extension of the Stoughton branch of the Providence/Stoughton Line .

The Full Build project would extend commuter rail service on the Stoughton Line to the New Bedford and Fall River lines, connecting more communities, including Easton and Raynham, to Boston . As proposed, Phase 2 would extend the Stoughton branch south over the abandoned Dighton and Somerset railroad through Easton, Raynham, and Taunton before meeting the Fall River/New Bedford Line at East Taunton .

However, funding has not yet been identified for the full build program . The project travels from Boston to Stoughton and continues south before splitting south of Taunton for Fall River and New Bedford (using the same southern alignment as Phase 1). Preliminary design is ongoing, and an anticipated service start date will be determined as the project advances .

### 6.2 Service Improvements

The MBTA and state transportation officials have discussed potential service improvements for the Fall River/New Bedford Line. These could include more frequent service, especially during peak commuting hours, and potential express service options that would reduce travel times for commuters .

Some riders have suggested that an express train would be a big help for commuters, as the current morning train takes a little over 90 minutes . The MBTA is evaluating various service enhancement options as ridership continues to grow.

## 7. Notable Riders and First Day Celebrations

The opening of the Fall River/New Bedford Line on March 24, 2025, was marked by significant celebration and emotional moments for the South Coast community. About 90 people boarded the first train from New Bedford to Boston at 4:27 a.m., the first to connect the cities in 67 years .

Among the notable riders was Brian da Camara of Fall River, who celebrated his 48th birthday by taking the first train out of Fall River in 65 years . He expressed excitement about not having to be stuck in traffic on the way to Celtics games and being able to get to Boston and back without driving .

Nine-year-old Kolson Miller convinced his father to wake up before 5 o'clock in the morning so they could watch the first train leave Fall River. He couldn't hold back a scream as the train's operator personally handed him an MBTA pin, saying "I'm so excited because this is history" .

The first day of service also attracted transit enthusiasts from across the region. Miles Taylor, a transit YouTuber, described the experience: "I want to say I was the first person to go over these tracks, or at least among the first. To me, New Bedford and Fall River are always these alien communities that were so difficult to get to. Now you have commuter rail service every 70 minutes all day. It just totally opens up the ability to take trips" .

## 8. Community Impact

### 8.1 Access to Services

The Fall River/New Bedford Line has significantly improved access to various services for South Coast residents. Dan Brogan, a public transit specialist for SRPEDD, said the new line not only builds connections between communities but also increases access to health care, including the VA medical center in Brockton .

Nancy Wilkinson and Al Lay, of Dartmouth, moved to the South Coast from Boston about 20 years ago. They had hoped the rail would arrive so that they could commute to work. Now that it's here, they're retired but plan to use it regularly for doctor appointments and to get together with friends .

### 8.2 Employment Opportunities

The line has created new opportunities for employment in both directions. Jeff Pontiff, a commercial real estate broker from New Bedford, hopes South Coast Rail will bring commuters in the other direction for work. "To me, it opens up the labor pool to come south to New Bedford to work, if we have enough industry," he said .

The line is also advantageous from a real-estate perspective, including opportunities for transit-oriented housing development. Pontiff noted that the train "adds to the overall aura of raising the bar of who we are as a community" .

### 8.3 Educational Access

The Fall River/New Bedford Line has expanded educational opportunities for students in both directions. More students from greater Boston and surrounding areas can easily commute to UMass Dartmouth, enhancing diversity and enrollment . Conversely, South Coast students now have easier access to colleges and universities in the Boston area.

## 9. Environmental Impact

The Fall River/New Bedford Line is expected to have positive environmental impacts by reducing automobile traffic on Route 24 and the Southeast Expressway. The line offers a convenient way to get to Boston while avoiding highway traffic .

The MBTA evaluated noise levels anticipated from South Coast Rail trains according to Federal Transit Administration (FTA) guidelines and detailed the results in the 2013 Final Environmental Impact Statement/Report and the 2018 Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Report . Based on this evaluation, the MBTA has provided funding for a set of alternative noise mitigation measures to owners of properties that are affected by noise above the impact level .

## 10. Connections and Integration

The Fall River/New Bedford Line connects with other MBTA services at several points along its route:

* **South Station**: Connects with the Red Line subway, commuter rail lines to Providence/Stoughton, Franklin/Foxboro, Kingston, and Greenbush, as well as intercity Amtrak services

* **JFK/UMass**: Connects with the Red Line subway

* **Quincy Center**: Connects with the Red Line subway

* **Braintree**: Connects with the Red Line subway

The line also provides connections to various bus routes at multiple stations, allowing for seamless transfers to local and regional bus services throughout the South Coast region.

## 11. Trivia and Interesting Facts

* The Fall River/New Bedford Line was formerly known as the Middleborough/Lakeville Line before being renamed on March 24, 2025 

* The Middleborough/Lakeville station has been renamed Lakeville station, with regular commuter rail service moving to the new Middleborough station on Grove Street

* The Lakeville station is now used only for seasonal CapeFlyer service to Cape Cod

* The line's southern terminus alternates between Fall River Depot and New Bedford stations

* The project cost more than \$1 billion to construct

* The first day of service coincided with the 65th anniversary of the line's closure in 1958

The project uses the Middleborough Secondary (currently a freight line) to provide service to Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River.
The Middleborough Secondary connects to Cotley Junction in East Taunton.
From Cotley Junction, Phase 1 trains join the New Bedford Main Line and continue to New Bedford.
From Cotley Junction, Phase 1 trains branch off on the Fall River Secondary to Fall River.
The area where trains branch off on the Fall River Secondary to Fall River is known as the Southern Triangle.
The MBTA uses EMD F40PH diesel-electric locomotives on the Fall River/New Bedford Line.
The F40PH is a 4-axle B-B locomotive with 3,000-3,200 horsepower (2.2-2.4 MW).
The F40PH was built by the Electro-Motive Division of General Motors between 1975 and 1992.
For passenger cars, the MBTA ordered 80 bilevel cars to provide immediate relief for the retirement of the MBB cars and for the completion of the South Coast Rail project.
The extension to Fall River and New Bedford alone required 16 new bilevel cars.
The first of the new bilevel cars arrived on MBTA property in late 2022.
All stations on the Fall River/New Bedford Line comply with MBTA standards and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements.
All stations on the Fall River/New Bedford Line include high-level platforms for "all-doors" boarding.
Other amenities at the stations include benches, canopies, bicycle storage, and parking facilities.
The new stations feature modern designs with accessible platforms, lighting, and passenger information systems.
Parking is available at many stations, with standard rates of $4 per day on weekdays and $2 per day on weekends/holidays.
The standard one-way fare for a trip from the South Coast stations to South Station is $12.25.
Reduced fare is $6 for riders who qualify.
Standard monthly passes are $388.
Reduced monthly passes are $190.
Children aged 11 and younger do not need a ticket.
Unlimited weekend passes are available for $10.
Riders can buy tickets on the MBTA's mTicket app, or with cash or card onboard the train.
For more information on buying tickets, the MBTA provides detailed guides on their website.
Parking is available at most stations on the Fall River/New Bedford Line.

During the promotional period following the line's opening, parking was free at six stations from March 24 until the end of day on April 30, 2025: Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Church Street, Fall River Depot, and New Bedford.
After the promotional period, standard parking rates apply: $4 per day on weekdays and $2 per day on weekends/holidays.
Overnight parking is allowed at most stations.
At New Bedford Station, overnight parking comes with a multi-day rate of $15 per day.
Parking can be paid for using the PayByPhone app at most MBTA lots.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line has had a significant impact on tourism in the South Coast region.
At the New Bedford Whaling Museum, ticket sales are up 30% compared to the previous year.
The increase in ticket sales at the New Bedford Whaling Museum is largely driven by Boston-area visitors.
President and CEO Amanda McMullen says the train is the only explanation for the sudden spike in ticket sales.

The extra admission revenue is helping to fund museum initiatives that are hard to find grants for, including upgrades to the ticket system and computer servers that support the museum's digital catalog.

The Whaling Museum has stepped up its advertising, using geographically targeted social media posts and video ad buys in Boston's South Station, the northernmost point on the Fall River/New Bedford Line.
South Coast Rail is anticipated to offer significant economic and housing development, as well as educational and recreational opportunities throughout southeastern Massachusetts.
Area residents will have much easier access to the many amenities of the South Coast and connections to downtown Boston due to South Coast Rail.
Boosting economic growth through increased access to Boston is expected to attract businesses, create jobs, and expand housing opportunities.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line is expanding educational access.
More students from greater Boston and surrounding areas are able to easily commute to UMass Dartmouth, enhancing diversity and enrollment.
New Bedford's new "transit-oriented development" zoning districts are designed to encourage development near the train stations.
A hotel to be built near New Bedford Station was approved.
Developers are showing increased interest in building housing near the stations.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line has experienced significant ridership growth.
On average, riders are taking 2,000 more trips each day compared to pre-extension levels.
Weekday ridership increased by 36%.
Weekend ridership increased by 13%.
Commuting workers, rather than leisure travelers, appear to make up most of the increased ridership.
This suggests the line is fulfilling its primary purpose of connecting South Coast residents to employment opportunities in Boston and other areas along the route.
The South Coast Rail project has a second phase, known as the "Full Build".
Phase 2 would turn the South Coast lines into an extension of the Stoughton branch of the Providence/Stoughton Line.
The Full Build project would extend commuter rail service on the Stoughton Line to the New Bedford and Fall River lines, connecting more communities, including Easton and Raynham, to Boston.

As proposed, Phase 2 would extend the Stoughton branch south over the abandoned Dighton and Somerset railroad through Easton, Raynham, and Taunton before meeting the Fall River/New Bedford Line at East Taunton.
Funding has not yet been identified for the full build program.
The project travels from Boston to Stoughton and continues south before splitting south of Taunton for Fall River and New Bedford (using the same southern alignment as Phase 1).
Preliminary design is ongoing for the project.
An anticipated service start date will be determined as the project advances.
The MBTA and state transportation officials have discussed potential service improvements for the Fall River/New Bedford Line.
Potential service improvements could include more frequent service, especially during peak commuting hours.
Potential service improvements could include express service options that would reduce travel times for commuters.
Some riders have suggested that an express train would be a big help for commuters, as the current morning train takes a little over 90 minutes.
The MBTA is evaluating various service enhancement options as ridership continues to grow.
The opening of the Fall River/New Bedford Line on March 24, 2025, was marked by significant celebration and emotional moments for the South Coast community.
About 90 people boarded the first train from New Bedford to Boston at 4:27 a.m.
The first train from New Bedford to Boston was the first to connect the cities in 67 years.
Among the notable riders was Brian da Camara of Fall River, who celebrated his 48th birthday by taking the first train out of Fall River in 65 years.
Brian da Camara expressed excitement about not having to be stuck in traffic on the way to Celtics games.
Brian da Camara expressed excitement about being able to get to Boston and back without driving.
Nine-year-old Kolson Miller convinced his father to wake up before 5 o'clock in the morning so they could watch the first train leave Fall River.
Kolson Miller couldn't hold back a scream as the train's operator personally handed him an MBTA pin.
Kolson Miller said "I'm so excited because this is history".
The first day of service also attracted transit enthusiasts from across the region.
Miles Taylor, a transit YouTuber, described the experience: "I want to say I was the first person to go over these tracks, or at least among the first."
Miles Taylor described the experience: "To me, New Bedford and Fall River are always these alien communities that were so difficult to get to."
Miles Taylor described the experience: "Now you have commuter rail service every 70 minutes all day."
Miles Taylor described the experience: "It just totally opens up the ability to take trips."
The Fall River/New Bedford Line has significantly improved access to various services for South Coast residents.

Dan Brogan, a public transit specialist for SRPEDD, said the new line not only builds connections between communities but also increases access to health care, including the VA medical center in Brockton.
Nancy Wilkinson and Al Lay, of Dartmouth, moved to the South Coast from Boston about 20 years ago.
Nancy Wilkinson and Al Lay had hoped the rail would arrive so that they could commute to work.
Now that the rail is here, Nancy Wilkinson and Al Lay are retired but plan to use it regularly for doctor appointments and to get together with friends.
The line has created new opportunities for employment in both directions.
Jeff Pontiff, a commercial real estate broker from New Bedford, hopes South Coast Rail will bring commuters in the other direction for work.
Jeff Pontiff stated, "To me, it opens up the labor pool to come south to New Bedford to work, if we have enough industry."
The line is also advantageous from a real-estate perspective, including opportunities for transit-oriented housing development.
Pontiff noted that the train "adds to the overall aura of raising the bar of who we are as a community".
The Fall River/New Bedford Line has expanded educational opportunities for students in both directions.
More students from greater Boston and surrounding areas can easily commute to UMass Dartmouth, enhancing diversity and enrollment.
South Coast students now have easier access to colleges and universities in the Boston area.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line is expected to have positive environmental impacts by reducing automobile traffic on Route 24 and the Southeast Expressway.
The line offers a convenient way to get to Boston while avoiding highway traffic.
The MBTA evaluated noise levels anticipated from South Coast Rail trains according to Federal Transit Administration (FTA) guidelines.
The MBTA detailed the results of noise level evaluation in the 2013 Final Environmental Impact Statement/Report and the 2018 Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Report.
Based on this evaluation, the MBTA has provided funding for a set of alternative noise mitigation measures to owners of properties that are affected by noise above the impact level.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line connects with other MBTA services at South Station.

At South Station, the Fall River/New Bedford Line connects with the Red Line subway, commuter rail lines to Providence/Stoughton, Franklin/Foxboro, Kingston, and Greenbush, as well as intercity Amtrak services.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line connects with other MBTA services at JFK/UMass.
At JFK/UMass, the Fall River/New Bedford Line connects with the Red Line subway.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line connects with other MBTA services at Quincy Center.
At Quincy Center, the Fall River/New Bedford Line connects with the Red Line subway.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line connects with other MBTA services at Braintree.
At Braintree, the Fall River/New Bedford Line connects with the Red Line subway.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line provides connections to various bus routes at multiple stations.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line allows for seamless transfers to local and regional bus services throughout the South Coast region.
The Fall River/New Bedford Line was formerly known as the Middleborough/Lakeville Line before being renamed on March 24, 2025.
The Middleborough/Lakeville station has been renamed Lakeville station.
Regular commuter rail service moved to the new Middleborough station on Grove Street.
The Lakeville station is now used only for seasonal CapeFlyer service to Cape Cod.
The line's southern terminus alternates between Fall River Depot and New Bedford stations.
The project cost more than $1 billion to construct.
The first day of service coincided with the 65th anniversary of the line's closure in 1958.

 March 24, 2025 

Residents of the South Coast are cheering on the return of passenger rail service after more than half a century with no trains connecting the region to Boston.

The MBTA’s new commuter rail line carries passengers from New Bedford, Fall River and Taunton to South Station in Boston. The three cities were previously the only major cities within 50 miles of Boston without commuter rail lines.

“It’s amazing,” said Brian da Camara. “When I heard, I was so psyched.”

The first day of service on Monday happened to fall on da Camara’s 48th birthday, and he used the opportunity to celebrate by testing out how long it will take him to get to Boston for NBA games.

“I don’t have to be stuck in traffic on the way to a Celtics game! Now we can get to Boston and back now without having to drive in a car and sticking in traffic,” he said.

The [Fall River/New Bedford line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable) is also welcome news for daily commuters like Katelyn Fisher, who took the train from the new Freetown station to Boston, where she works in-person five days a week.

“It’s really cool to see an opportunity for people who live way down here to make their way up to Boston,” she said.

![Image 7: Two women sit on a train](https://cdn.grove.wgbh.org/dims4/default/3f3d65f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x3024+0+0/resize/723x542!/quality/70/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fk1-prod-gbh.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcf%2Fcd%2Fef651ed84d75b4b878b70b006315%2Fkaitlyn.jpg)

Katelyn Fisher (right) and Angela Flanagan on the new South Coast rail service, Monday, March 24, 2025.

 Jeremy Siegel  GBH News 

Train enthusiasts of all ages were also on hand for the launch. Nine-year-old Kolson Miller convinced his father to wake up before 5 o’clock in the morning so they could watch the first train leave Fall River. He couldn’t hold back a scream as the train’s operator personally handed him an MBTA pin.

“I’m so excited because this is history,” Kolson said. “What I would say to the people who made this happen is, thank you so much.”

![Image 8: A young boy stands outside of a train](https://cdn.grove.wgbh.org/dims4/default/dbfd028/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x3024+0+0/resize/723x542!/quality/70/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fk1-prod-gbh.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F09%2Fa2dff19743998285a1bbb8f83339%2Fkolson.jpg)

Nine-year-old Kolson Miller at Fall River Depot Station

 Jeremy Siegel/GBH News 

The long-awaited project cost the T more than $1 billion to construct. The Fall River/New Bedford line stops at 15 stations, including six new rail stops. Trains run every 70 minutes on weekdays and every two hours on weekends.

The scheduled trip time from Fall River and New Bedford to Boston is roughly 90 minutes, which is generally faster than car travel during rush hour. For Somerset resident Michael Kimpel, who drives his daughter to college in Boston four days a week, that’s a welcome relief.

“I’ll save some gas money,” he said.

![Image 9: A man and a woman stand outside of a train](https://cdn.grove.wgbh.org/dims4/default/27a7f08/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x3024+0+0/resize/723x542!/quality/70/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fk1-prod-gbh.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd7%2F6d%2F9732bb1240cea98b3ba84521188c%2Fmichael.jpg)

Michael and Victoria Kimpell at Fall River Depot Station

 Jeremy Siegel/GBH News 

Kimpel’s daughter, Victoria Kimpel, is also excited to be able to do school assignments on the train — too precarious a task, she said, for the car.

“I’m able to really sit back, enjoy and do my work,” she said.

To encourage ridership, all rides on the Fall River/New Bedford line will be free through the end of March. Fare-free service will continue only on weekends through April. Free parking is also available at many stations through April.

For the first time ever, MBTA commuter rail trains will start carrying passengers on South Coast Rail this Monday.

The first train is scheduled to leave New Bedford Station at 4:27 a.m., stopping at Church Street Station at 4:33 a.m. and arriving at Boston’s South Station at 6:01 a.m.

Later on Monday morning, state and local officials will board special trains from New Bedford and Fall River, meeting in East Taunton for a kickoff celebration at 10 a.m. Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll will board in New Bedford with Mayor Jon Mitchell, while Gov. Maura Healey and MBTA General Manager Phil Eng will depart from Fall River.

![Image 7: Purple commuter rail train approaches a platform with a yellow safety line at a station](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/New-Bedford-Station-test-train-scaled-b-edited.jpg?resize=780%2C437&ssl=1)

Fares [will be free](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-mbta-announce-free-south-coast-rail-service-through-the-end-of-march) for South Coast riders every day through the end of March, then every weekend through the end of April. Parking at South Coast stations will be free every day through the end of April.

Now, New Bedford will have a rail connection to Boston for the first time since 1958, when the New Haven Railroad closed the South Coast train route it had run for a century.

The city has waited decades for this MBTA extension to open. Roughly half of New Bedford’s population is too young to remember a time before officials started [promising](https://newbedfordlight.org/key-points-on-the-route-to-south-coast-rail-2/#:~:text=1991%3A%20Gov.%20Bill%20Weld%20promises%20South%20Coast%20rail%20by%201997) commuter rail service for the region in the early 1990s.

The project had many stops and starts as officials gathered funding and deliberated over possible routes.

The most recent groundbreaking took place in 2019, after the state settled on a plan to connect South Coast cities to the existing Middleborough/Lakeville line, dodging a more difficult and expensive option to build tracks through the Hockomock Swamp toward the Stoughton line. That more direct route is still planned as “phase two” of the project, to be completed in the 2030s.

Even after construction began, the project faced more delays. Its schedule was in limbo as recently as [last spring](https://newbedfordlight.org/another-delay-for-start-of-south-coast-rail/), after the MBTA scrapped opening dates scheduled for late 2023 and summer 2024.

The MBTA then targeted May 2025 as its launch date. But it finished safety testing ahead of schedule, and in February [announced](https://newbedfordlight.org/south-coast-rail-coming-march-24/) that the project was sprinting toward a March 24 launch. Local officials scrambled to make arrangements for [public transit](https://newbedfordlight.org/srta-rushing-to-prep-for-south-coast-rail/) and [parking](https://newbedfordlight.org/how-to-get-to-the-south-coast-rail-stations-in-new-bedford/#:~:text=The%20Port%20Authority%20released%20information%20on%20its%20separate%20parking%20system%20Monday%20night.).

Starting on March 24, the Middleboro/Lakeville commuter rail line will be renamed the Fall River/New Bedford line. New Bedford has two new stations — one near downtown, and another on Church Street in the North End. New stations are also opening in Fall River, Freetown, and Middleborough on Monday.

On Thursday, the MBTA [announced](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-mbta-announce-free-south-coast-rail-service-through-the-end-of-march) that fares will be free for passengers riding to or from South Coast stations through the end of March. This expands [a promotion](https://newbedfordlight.org/free-weekend-rides-planned-to-lure-south-coast-rail-users/) that includes free fares on weekends through the end of April, including the Patriots’ Day holiday on Monday, April 21. All you need to do is inform the conductor of your origin and destination.

As part of the promotion, parking is also free at South Coast stations every day through the end of April.

After the promotion ends, the standard fare for a one-way trip to South Station will be $12.25. Reduced fare will be $6 for [riders who qualify](https://newbedfordlight.org/how-do-i-buy-tickets-for-the-south-coast-rail/#:~:text=How%20do%20I%20qualify%20for%20free%20or%20reduced%20fare%3F). Standard monthly passes are $388, and reduced monthly passes are $190. Children aged 11 and younger don’t need a ticket. [Unlimited weekend passes](https://www.mbta.com/fares/commuter-rail-weekends) will be available for $10. The passes also work on some holidays.

Parking will cost $4 a day on weekdays. When the free parking promotion is over at the end of April, parking will be $2 on weekends. Overnight parking is allowed, but at New Bedford Station it will come with a multi-day rate of $15 per day.

Riders can buy tickets on the MBTA’s [mTicket app](https://www.mbta.com/mbta-endorsed-apps), or with cash or card onboard the train. For more information, see [our guide to buying tickets](https://newbedfordlight.org/how-do-i-buy-tickets-for-the-south-coast-rail/).

Direct rides from downtown New Bedford to Boston’s South Station will generally take 94 to 98 minutes, [the schedule shows](https://newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/SCR-Schedule-March-2025-1.pdf). Some trips that include a transfer will take nearly two hours.

Inbound trains will leave New Bedford Station from 4:27 a.m. to 9:23 p.m., with 14 total departing trains throughout the day. Outbound trains from South Station will have weekday departures from 6:45 a.m. to 11:59 p.m.

On weekends, inbound trains will leave New Bedford Station from 4:47 a.m. to 9:53 p.m., with seven departures throughout the day. Outbound trains will leave South Station from 6:37 a.m. to 11:59 p.m.

Some trips will require a transfer at East Taunton Station. That’s because the MBTA will run “shuttle trains” adding extra service along the two branches of the route without clogging up the rails north of Taunton. Check out [our explainer on shuttle trains](https://newbedfordlight.org/whats-a-shuttle-train/).

4.title: About the South Coast Rail project
4.description: Learn about the South Coast Rail project
4.content:
Project Overview
----------------

South Coast Rail will be built in phases. Phase 1 service will provide a one-seat ride by extending the existing Middleborough/Lakeville commuter rail service from Boston to Taunton, Fall River and New Bedford.

Elements of Phase 1:

*   Uses the Middleborough Secondary (currently a freight line) to provide service to Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River. The Middleborough Secondary connects to Cotley Junction in East Taunton.
*   From Cotley Junction, Phase 1 trains will join the New Bedford Main Line and continue to New Bedford, or they will branch off on the Fall River Secondary to Fall River (this area is known as the Southern Triangle).

Benefits of Phase 1:

*   Reconstructs 12.1 miles of the Fall River Secondary
*   Reconstructs 24.1 miles of Middleborough Secondary and the New Bedford Main Line.
*   Improves freight service to the region and will provide redundancy for commuter rail riders once the Full Build is operating.

The Full Build Project will travel on the Stoughton Main Line and Northeast Corridor (north of Canton Junction). The Full Build presents more challenges related to wetland impacts, complex engineering, electrification and cost.

Phase 1 and Full Build
----------------------

To provide service to southeastern Massachusetts, South Coast Rail will be constructed in phases.

### Phase 1 Project

*   Extends Commuter Rail service on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line to New Bedford, Fall River, and Taunton.
*   Phase 1 is fully funded with $1B in State revenue bonds, and construction is complete.

### Full Build Project

*   Extends Commuter Rail service on the Stoughton Line to the New Bedford and Fall River lines, connecting more communities, including Easton and Raynham, to Boston.
*   Funding has not yet been identified for the Full Build program.

For more details, see the Phase 1 and Full Build [corridor maps](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/south-coast-rail-project-corridor-maps).

Phase 1 station locations
-------------------------

Phase 1 will continue service to nine existing stations on the Middleborough/Lakeville line and will add six new stations including:

*   Middleborough
*   East Taunton
*   Freetown
*   Fall River Depot
*   Church Street in New Bedford
*   New Bedford

For the exact locations of each station see the Phase 1 and Full Build [corridor maps](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/south-coast-rail-project-corridor-maps).

All stations will comply with MBTA standards and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements, which include high-level platforms for "all-doors" boarding. Other amenities will include benches, canopies, bicycle storage and parking.

Phase 1 projected service
-------------------------

(subject to change)| Line | Original Project Commitment | MBTA Delivery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| East Taunton-South Station | **26** | **32** |
| Fall River Line | **13** | **15** |
| New Bedford Line | **13** | **17** |
| Weekends | **-** | **26** |

*Direct trips to/from South Station*

*   In addition to direct service, there will also be shuttles operating between each terminus point and East Taunton Station; this allows for even more frequent service, which is consistent with the All Day Service model across the rest of the Commuter Rail network
*   Weekday Direct service will run approximately every 70 minutes
*   Weekend Direct service will run approximately every 120 minutes
*   Late Night Service will be offered to South Coast Rail stations with the last train leaving Boston just before mid-night

Noise program eligibility
-------------------------

MassDOT evaluated noise levels anticipated from South Coast Rail trains according to Federal Transit Administration (FTA) guidelines and detailed the results in the [2013 Final Environmental Impact Statement/Report](https://www.mass.gov/lists/south-coast-rail-documents-and-meeting-materials#full-build-final-environmental-impact-statement/report-(feis/r)---august-2013-) and the [2018 Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Report](https://www.mass.gov/lists/south-coast-rail-documents-and-meeting-materials#phase-1-final-supplemental-environmental-impact-report-(fseir)---april-2018-). While freight trains currently operate along the existing railroad corridor, they are infrequent. The Commuter Rail trains will run multiple trips every day, which creates additional noise. The MBTA developed and implemented a noise mitigation program based on the FTA standards.

Based on this program, the MBTA has provided funding for a set of alternative noise mitigation measures to owners of properties that are affected by noise above the impact level. See the[South Coast Rail Noise Program Frequently Asked Questions](https://www.mass.gov/doc/scr-noise-mitigation-program-faq/download) for more information.

Construction impacts, timeline and contracts
--------------------------------------------

### Early Action Construction

MassDOT began Early Action construction projects in 2019 on South Coast Rail to prepare for the larger Phase 1 main line rail construction contracts. The first visible active construction projects were drainage culvert replacement and a major railroad grade crossing update in New Bedford. This work also included the construction of 5 wetland mitigation areas in the corridor and was substantially completed in Summer 2020. Additional work to replace four railroad bridges was completed in Fall 2020. The Early Action took place in Berkley, Fall River, Freetown, Lakeville, Middleborough, New Bedford, Raynham, and Taunton.

More information can be found on the [SCR Construction Activity](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/south-coast-rail-construction-activity) page.

### Early Demolition Contract

The Early Demolition contract was awarded to DW White Construction of Acushnet and was completed in Fall 2020. This work involved the demolition of buildings and other structures located on MBTA controlled property at nine separate locations in Middleborough, Taunton, Berkley, Freetown, Fall River, and New Bedford.

### Fall River Secondary Line Construction

This construction contract was [awarded to Skanska DW White JV](https://www.mbta.com/news/2020-05-11/fmcb-approves-159-million-contract-south-coast-rail-main-line-construction) on May 11, 2020. Work on the Fall River Secondary will include track, stations, bridges, and a layover facility. Construction began Summer 2020 and is complete.

### New Bedford, Middleborough, Signal and Communications Contract

This construction contract was [awarded to SCR Constructors JV](https://www.mbta.com/news/2020-08-24/fmcb-approves-4035-million-contract-south-coast-rail-main-line-construction) on August 24, 2020. Work on the New Bedford Main Line to the Middleborough Secondary includes track, stations, bridges, a layover facility, and the signal and communications systems for all of Phase 1. Construction began in fall 2020 and is complete.

Public outreach
---------------

The South Coast Rail team has conducted numerous public meetings across the Phase 1 project communities. The project team will continue to meet with the cities and towns as needed.

In addition to specific railroad safety measures, education is a key factor in addressing community safety. The South Coast Rail Project funded the development of instructive videos for railroad safety, geared to schools and the general public. This effort is supplemented by Operation Lifesaver volunteers. MassDOT and the MBTA work regularly with[Operation Lifesaver](https://oli.org/), a national program sponsored by the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA), that provides community railroad safety education programs.

The MBTA and Keolis, the MBTA’s Commuter Rail operator, has been working with South Coast Rail community first responders to conduct regular emergency response drills and training.

Updated Oct. 25, 2021, 7:48 a.m. ET

[The South Coast Rail](https://www.mbta.com/projects/south-coast-rail) project promises to bring passenger train service back to Fall River for the first time in more than 60 years. The path to this point has been fraught with detours, false starts, ever-increasing price tags, and broken promises.

The rail project, which started as a proposal in 1991, has passed through the hands of six governors and seen its cost rise by a factor of 25, from $136 million to $3.4 billion.

Let's take a look at how Fall River and the Southcoast had access to passenger rail, lost it, and [is fighting to get it back.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/story/business/transportation/2021/03/02/commuter-rail-construction-work-fall-river-kicking-into-gear-south-coast-depot-bridges-layover/6865840002/)

[![Image 1](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/22/NHER/352f8a79-df93-4e08-b62c-2978618959ca-Photo_Oct_14_5_31_59_PM.jpg?crop=5183,2916,x0,y263&width=660&height=372&format=pjpg&auto=webp)](https://www.southbendtribune.com/picture-gallery/business/transportation/2021/10/25/fall-river-tour-south-coast-rail-station-construction-freetown-fiola-mbta/6129964001/)

Fall River's place in transportation history 
---------------------------------------------

**1844-1854:** Col. Richard Borden builds the city's first railroad in 1844, the Fall River Branch Railroad, linking Fall River with Myricks Junction in Berkley. By 1846, it and two other railroad companies have merged to form the Fall River Railroad, with connections up to Boston. In 1847, the Fall River Railroad starts offering steamship service to New York City, a service that was known as the Fall River Line. The company merged again, this time with Old Colony Railroad, to form Old Colony and Fall River Railroad in 1854.

![Image 2: A postcard of Fall River Station from the early 20th century.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/836848db-164e-402c-8916-f733cd728570-fall_river_station.jpg?width=660&height=420&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**1854-1958:** Old Colony has an extensive network of rail lines across the region, connecting Fall River by train with places like Providence, New Bedford, the Cape, and Boston. The entire Old Colony system falls under the control of the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad Co. in 1893, giving it a monopoly over transportation in the entire region. In the first half of the 20th century, the rail line undergoes a period of decline due to economic turmoil and competition from the increasingly affordable automobile. The Fall River Line steamship service, once the most famous and luxurious method of travel on the East Coast, is liquidated in 1937. Amid bankruptcy during the Great Depression, Old Colony tries in 1938 to abandon unprofitable lines and 93 stations, including Fall River’s Ferry Street station, but this is reversed in a decision that reaches the Supreme Court in 1939. But the Old Colony rail service in Fall River, along with Taunton and New Bedford will only last less than another 20 years – in 1958, rail service to these cities ends.

**1950s-1960s:** As commercial passenger rail fell into decline, [the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://www.mbta.com/) begins subsidizing railroad companies and then buying commuter rail lines. Over the years, the MBTA returns service to areas that had seen service end. Meanwhile, expressways are built and expanded to connect the Southcoast north -- Route 24 carries Fall River traffic north, while Route 140 connects New Bedford to Taunton and Route 24.

![Image 3: A view of the Fall River Line terminal in New York City from 1937.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/dcb9c19d-3e1a-4f1c-96e0-147055431367-Fall_River_line_pier.jpg?width=660&height=537&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Weld's promise kicks off the South Coast Rail push
--------------------------------------------------

**March 1991:** Gov. William Weld asks the state Legislature authorize the sale of MBTA bonds to pay for preliminary engineering and environmental studies to extend commuter rail from Stoughton to southeastern Massachusetts, including Fall River. He’s so confident it will happen under his watch that in February 1992 he proclaims, “Sue me if it doesn’t happen.”

**June 1995:** Anne Galbraith, an MBTA project manager, tells people at a Fall River public hearing that commuters could be boarding trains for Boston by the end of 1997 under a best-case scenario. In a press conference the next month in New Bedford, he promises rail from Fall River and New Bedford to Boston by the fall of 1997.

![Image 4: Former Massachusetts Gov. William Weld poses for a portrait in 2020. Weld served as the governor of Massachusetts from 1991 to 1997.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/presto/2020/01/08/PDEM/5a4b64e8-b53a-466b-8cb3-bf4611c788ac-RS_Weld_010620_.jpg?width=660&height=440&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**August 1996:** Weld signs a transportation bond bill that includes $136 million to extend commuter rail.

**March-April 1997:** The MBTA releases a study saying the cost to bring commuter rail to Fall River will be closer to $430 million, more than three times the initial estimates. Then-state Rep. Robert Correia says in an interview, “I honestly see it happening. It’s just a question of time.” He suggests the project would likely be up and running by spring of 1999.

**July 1997:** Weld resigns as governor to focus on what becomes an unsuccessful attempt to become ambassador to Mexico. Paul Cellucci becomes governor, and says he is committed to extending rail to Fall River and New Bedford.

![Image 5: In this undated file photo, a commuter train leaves the Middleboro/Lakeville Station on the Old Colony Rail line.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/presto/2021/02/03/NENT/e87ee26b-41ed-4f04-a005-b2b2cca9574d-Middleboro-Lakeville_station_Commuter_Rail_train.jpg?width=660&height=439&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Running out of money, and running into a swamp
----------------------------------------------

**September 1997:** The MBTA’s Old Colony commuter rail line opens, extending service to Middleboro/Lakeville.

**March-April 1998:** The Executive Office of Transportation and Construction authorizes $20 million for the commuter rail design phase. Soon afterward, the House Transportation Committee approves a bill instructing the MBTA to begin construction on a commuter rail extension to Fall River.

**October 1998:** A groundbreaking ceremony is held at the railroad bridge on Turner Street in Fall River for the proposed commuter rail system.

**November 1999:** State Secretary of Environmental Affairs Robert Durand blasts the plan to extend commuter rail to Fall River from Stoughton, saying it would cut through Hockomock Swamp, harm at least six rare species and affect one of the largest and most significant freshwater wetlands in the commonwealth. He’s supported by residents of Raynham and Easton, who fight the extension.

![Image 6: A view of the Hockomock Swamp.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/-mm-/15c99ac303d681770c92d74529048fe3a8184b72/c=0-30-600-368/local/-/media/2020/10/31/Quincy/ghows_gallery-WL-103109999-8ff19cd1.jpg?width=600&height=338&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**January 2000:** With Gov. Paul Cellucci restating his commitment to extending commuter rail to Fall River, state officials release a new timeline indicating construction will begin by fall 2002 and be completed by 2004.

**July 2002:** The MBTA pushes project start date back to 2007 because it has no money to fund the construction. By now, estimates of the project’s cost have risen from just over $400 million to more than $600 million.

**May 2003:** The MBTA asks the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to halt the environmental permitting process while Gov. Mitt Romney analyzes the cost of the rail extension.

**March-June 2004:** The MBTA does not include funding for an extension to Fall River in its 2004-2009 capital investment plan. Fall River officials meet with Romney, but the governor refuses to commit to bringing rail to Fall River. He eventually agrees to support the rail project in exchange for Fall River lawmakers supporting a project to expand the Sagamore rotary on Cape Cod.

**August 2004:** Romney authorizes more than $430 million for the rail project, though $425 million of that will be released only if the federal government matches it.

**March-April 2005:** Romney releases a long-term transportation plan that includes $670 million for rail to Fall River and New Bedford, and estimates building the extension will take six to eight years. He declares the rail extension is “going to get done” but cautions that it will take more work.

Price tag soars as MBTA focuses on going electric 
--------------------------------------------------

**June 2005:** Douglas Foy, chief of commonwealth development, testifies before the joint committee on Bonding, Capital Expenditures and State Assets that the project’s estimated price tag could now be as high as $1 billion.

![Image 7: Then-Mayor Will Flanagan, center, and Gov. Deval Patrick view track repair work on the Fall River section of the Mass Coastal Railroad in 2014.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/7a15e8b1-84b5-4187-94cf-cbcb324810c9-deval_patrick.jpg?width=660&height=493&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**April 2007:** Gov. Deval Patrick releases “South Coast Rail: A Plan for Action,” detailing the steps that will be taken to bring commuter rail to Fall River and New Bedford. Patrick says the project’s estimated price tag is now $1.4 billion, and that trains will be rolling by December 2016.

**August 2009:** Patrick unveils his $1.4 billion plan to build a long-promised commuter rail project linking New Bedford and Fall River to Boston, saying it would create up to 3,800 permanent jobs by the year 2030 and generate nearly $500 million in economic activity.

**September 2009:** State finalizes a deal with CSX to purchase rail lines in New Bedford and Fall River.

**January 2013:** Patrick unveils another new state transportation plan that calls for spending $10 billion over 10 years, including the South Coast Rail line between Fall River and Boston by 2021 -- by now, with a $1.8 billion estimated price tag.

![Image 8: The MBTA train depot in Stoughton.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/-mm-/b46158a8388b70656aad27c7567a0c37ef8e405c/c=0-126-2500-1532/local/-/media/2020/11/02/WickedLocal/ghows-WL-201007962-2030c47e.jpg?width=660&height=372&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**June 2013:** The Army Corps of Engineers determines a route to the Southcoast from Stoughton using electric trains will have the least environmental impact. A state report identifies this route as the preferred route for South Coast Rail.

**June 2014:** MassDOT awards a 10-year contract for up to $210 million for South Coast Rail. Patrick hails this as “a game changer” to move the project from the planning to construction stage. By now, the price tag has risen to an estimated $2.3 billion.

**November 2014-January 2016:** The South Coast Rail project pushes slowly forward as seven railroad freight bridges are replaced.

![Image 9: Phase 1 of the South Coast Rail plan will continue service from Middleboro, splitting in Berkley to separate lines going to Fall River and New Bedford.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/d16137ba-7ef2-4481-99aa-c00207c082b5-map.jpg?width=660&height=325&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Back to the drawing board, and South Coast Rail gets a two-part plan
--------------------------------------------------------------------

**June 2016:** MassDOT and the MBTA say that by now, the cost of South Coast Rail using electric trains from Stoughton has risen to $3.4 billion, and the construction schedule would need to be delayed another seven years. Given that development, they revisit a previously rejected plan – to extend the rail line from Middleboro/Lakeville using diesel trains, saying that it would cost a lot less and be constructed sooner.

**March 2017:** Gov. Charlie Baker’s administration agrees on a new course for South Coast Rail. Phase 1 would continue diesel train service from Middleboro/Lakeville, splitting at Myricks Junction for separate lines to Fall River and New Bedford, at a cost of just over $1 billion. The project is slated to start in 2019 and be complete by 2024. Meanwhile, engineering, design and permitting work will continue on the “full build” of the South Coast Rail project – electric rail service from Stoughton, estimated to cost over $3 billion and be complete by 2030.

![Image 10: After years of waiting, Gov. Charlie Baker, along with many other state and local politicians, break ground on South Coast Rail off of Chace Road in Freetown in 2019.](https://www.southbendtribune.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/4083c9e3-00d9-4587-83e7-7d9f3a79f89e-groundbreaking.jpg?width=660&height=454&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**June 2019:** Baker and political leaders from across the region meet in Freetown for a groundbreaking ceremony.

**2019-2021:** Construction continues on the South Coast Rail project, which includes making rail improvements, rebuilding rail bridges, building two new layover facilities in Fall River and New Bedford, and building and six new stations. MBTA officials say the project remains on schedule and on budget, and is expected to be running by the end of 2023.

7.content:
La **EMD F40PH** es una locomotora diésel-eléctrica B-B de cuatro ejes y 3.000–3.200 hp (2,2–2,4 MW) construida por la División Electro-Motive de General Motors en varias variantes entre 1975 y 1992. Para su uso en las rutas de pasajeros de corta distancia de Amtrak, se convirtió en la columna vertebral de la flota diésel de Amtrak después del fracaso del EMD SDP40F. El F40PH también encontró un uso generalizado en los ferrocarriles de cercanías en los Estados Unidos y con VIA Rail en Canadá. Morrison-Knudsen y MotivePower fabricaron variantes adicionales de la F40PH entre 1988 y 1998, en su mayoría reconstruidas a partir de locomotoras más antiguas.

Amtrak retiró su flota de F40PH a principios de la década de 2000 en favor de la GE Genesis, pero la locomotora sigue siendo el pilar de los trenes de larga distancia de VIA Rail; En el reverso del billete de 10 dólares canadienses de la serie Frontier aparece una representación de la locomotora que transporta _The Canadian_. Los F40PH siguen siendo comunes en muchos otros ferrocarriles de cercanías en todo Estados Unidos. Además, Amtrak ha mantenido 22 de sus F40PH en uso como unidades de control sin motor.

Fondo
-----

Amtrak heredó una flota de locomotoras diésel envejecida y mecánicamente incompatible de varios ferrocarriles privados en su puesta en marcha en 1971. Las locomotoras más modernas permanecieron en manos privadas para el servicio de carga, o para operar los diversos servicios de conmutación que, por ley, no pasaron a Amtrak. Para reemplazar estos Amtrak ordenó 150 locomotoras EMD SDP40F, que comenzaron a entrar en servicio en 1973. Estos fueron complementados por 25 GE P30CHs que entraron en servicio en 1975. El SDP40F fue un diseño problemático; problemas con la distribución de peso llevaron a una serie de descarriles a mediados de los años 70. Mientras tanto, el mal diseño de camiones del P30CH (y el GE E60CP eléctrico) restringió nuevas órdenes de esa unidad cuando Amtrak se encontró necesitando más potencia de distancia corta y mediana en la primavera de 1975.

Diseño
------

[![Image 1: Blue locomotive on raised track](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Metra_Locomotive_EMD_F40PHM-2.jpg/220px-Metra_Locomotive_EMD_F40PHM-2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Metra_Locomotive_EMD_F40PHM-2.jpg)

Metra EMD F40PHM-2 No. 206 cerca de Stuart Field en Chicago, Illinois

El diseño de la F40PH se basó en la locomotora EMD GP40-2 y compartió el cilindro EMD 645E3 V16 de la locomotora, motor diesel de dos tiempos y refrigerado por agua (impulsión de presión). El motor principal desarrolló 3000 hp (2.2 MW) a 893 RPM. El generador principal (tracción) convierte la energía mecánica del motor principal a la electricidad distribuida a través de un gabinete de alta tensión a los motores de tracción. Cada uno de los cuatro motores de tracción está orientado a un par de ruedas de conducción; la relación de engranaje determina la velocidad máxima de la locomotora. Un F40PH estándar tiene una relación de marcha de 57:20, lo que permite una velocidad máxima de 103 mph (166 km/h). Algunos Amtrak F40 PH fueron entregados con un 56:21 engranaje para 110 mph (177 km/h). Las primeras 30 locomotoras fueron construidas con un tanque de combustible de 1.500 dólares EE.UU. (5.700 L; 1.200 imp gal). Las unidades posteriores fueron construidas con un tanque de 1.800-US-gallón (6.800 L; 1.500 imp gal). Comienzo con el **EMD F40PH-2**, introducido en 1985, el impulsor principal desarrolló 3.200 caballos de fuerza (2.4 MW). Muchos de los F40PH originales fueron actualizados para coincidir con esa salida. Las locomotoras tenían 56 pies de 2 pulgadas (17.12 m) de largo. Un F40PH estándar pesa 260,000 lb (120.000 kg).

Para el servicio de pasajeros, el F40PH tiene otro alternador eléctrico, el generador de cabecera. La unidad HEP genera energía CA trifásica a 480 V (500 kW en el primer pedido, 800 kW en unidades posteriores) para iluminación, calefacción y aire acondicionado del tren. Originalmente, los F40PH alimentaban el alternador HEP desde el motor primario. Como resultado de eso, el tren tenía que estar a una frecuencia constante de 60 Hz y el motor principal tenía que girar a una velocidad constante de 893 RPM mientras suministraba potencia al extremo de cabecera (incluso parado, con el acelerador en ralentí). La potencia de los motores de tracción se controlaba variando la excitación de campo del generador principal (de tracción). En algunas versiones posteriores de la F40PH (y en muchas F40 reconstruidas), un segundo pequeño motor diésel auxiliar en la parte trasera de la locomotora alimenta el alternador HEP. En estos motores, la velocidad del motor primario varía de la forma habitual. Se identifican por el escape diésel en la parte trasera de la locomotora y por su silencioso ralentí. Los F40 restantes, con motores primarios de RPM constantes, son notablemente más ruidosos.

En el diseño inicial, la caja de la batería y los depósitos de aire estaban ubicados delante del tanque de combustible. En las locomotoras fabricadas después de 1977, éstas se colocaron detrás del tanque. La caja de la batería volvió a su ubicación original en el F40PH-2. Los F40PH-2 entregados a Caltrain incorporaron faros estilo Southern Pacific Railroad.

La designación "F40PH" fue la siguiente: "F" para el cuerpo de vacuno de ancho completo, "40" como la locomotora es parte de las 40 series de EMD (basado en la locomotora de carga GP40-2), "P" para el servicio de pasajeros, y "H" para la potencia de cabeza.

Historia
--------

[![Image 2: An Amtrak train runs beside a road](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/AMTK_257_at_Agnew_june_1980xRP.jpg/220px-AMTK_257_at_Agnew_june_1980xRP.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AMTK_257_at_Agnew_june_1980xRP.jpg)

Amtrak EMD F40PHR No. 257 liderando el _Coast Starlight_ en Agnew en 1980, seguido de un par de EMD SDP40Fs

[![Image 3: Passenger train rounding a bend, with snow-capped mountains in background](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Thecanadiannearjasper.jpg/220px-Thecanadiannearjasper.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thecanadiannearjasper.jpg)

Reconstruido VIA Rail F40PH-2D No. 6434 liderando el _Canadian_ cerca de Jasper, Alberta en 2011, con una unidad original

Amtrak encargó sus primeras 30 EMD F40PH el 8 de mayo de 1975. La primera de las nuevas locomotoras entró en servicio el 9 de abril de 1976. Amtrak pretendía que las locomotoras fueran para rutas cortas como la _San Diego_ en Servicios de California y del Corredor Noreste en la parte de la ruta que entonces no estaba electrificada entre New Haven, Connecticut y Boston, Massachusetts.

Las rutas de larga distancia estaban protegidas por los entonces nuevos EMD SDP40F, descritos por J. David Ingles a finales de 1975 como las "estrellas de los trenes de larga distancia de Amtrak". Sin embargo, dos eventos llevaron a un cambio importante en la forma de pensar dentro de Amtrak con respecto al EMD SDP40F. El primer evento fue una fuerte caída en la confiabilidad mecánica del EMD SDP40F, incluidos varios descarrilamientos. El segundo evento fue el invierno inusualmente duro de 1976-1977, que dejó de lado a muchos de los viejos autocares calentados por vapor de Amtrak. Amtrak suspendió numerosas rutas y puso en servicio los nuevos autocares Amfleet I equipados con HEP, diseñados para recorridos cortos. El F40PH, con su generador HEP incorporado, fue la elección natural para transportar estos autocares. A medida que aumentaron los problemas con el EMD SDP40F, Amtrak adoptó el F40PH como su solución a largo plazo en todo el país para el servicio de motores diésel.

En la primavera de 1977, Amtrak intercambió 40 EMD SDP40F de nuevo con EMD. Los componentes, incluido el motor primario, se instalaron en un marco EMD F40PH. Las 40 locomotoras reconstruidas, denominadas **F40PHR**, eran idénticas a las EMD F40PH de nueva construcción, incorporando el tanque de combustible más grande y el generador HEP más potente que se había convertido en estándar.

Amtrak finalmente adquirió 132 F40PHR de esta manera, lo que combinado con nuevos pedidos entre 1975 y 1988 y con la compra de seis GMD F40PH de GO Transit en 1990, dio como resultado una flota de 216 locomotoras, la más grande del país. flota.

El primer operador de trenes de cercanías que encargó F40PH fue la Autoridad de Transporte Regional (RTA) de Chicago, precursora de Metra, que encargó 74 entre 1977 y 1983. Metra encargó 41 más entre 1988 y 1992. Otras agencias que compraron el F40PH incluía la Autoridad de Tránsito de la Bahía de Massachusetts (MBTA) (18), Caltrain (20), GO Transit (6), New Jersey Transit (17) y VIA Rail (59). Finalmente, la empresa de construcción ferroviaria Speno encargó cuatro. En total, EMD construyó 449 locomotoras, incluidas las F40PHR de intercambio.

[![Image 4: GO Transit train #510 traveling along a track with signal lights visible](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Eleven_Shots_of_Canadian_Passenger_Trains_in_Toronto%2C_March_1981%2C_by_Roger_Puta_%2833895023751%29.jpg/220px-Eleven_Shots_of_Canadian_Passenger_Trains_in_Toronto%2C_March_1981%2C_by_Roger_Puta_%2833895023751%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eleven_Shots_of_Canadian_Passenger_Trains_in_Toronto,_March_1981,_by_Roger_Puta_(33895023751).jpg)

GO Transit F40PH 510 on the CN Kingston Subdivision in March 1981

El F40PH funcionó bien para Amtrak: a principios de la década de 1990 sólo cuatro habían sido retirados debido a accidentes. La locomotora estaba en el centro de la publicidad de Amtrak. La revista _Trains_ estimó que, de media, cada F40PH viajaba hasta 175.000 millas (282.000 km) al año.

Amtrak comenzó a reemplazar el F40PH con el GE Dash 8-32BWH en 1991, el GE P40DC en 1993 y el GE P42DC en 1996. Todos fueron retirados en 2001 con la llegada del último P42DC, y su última asignación regular fue en el _Maple Leaf_ en diciembre de 2001. El Ferrocarril del Canal de Panamá adquirió varios F40PH antiguos de Amtrak para servicio de carga y pasajeros; la potencia de cabecera de 480 V coincidía con el voltaje utilizado por la refrigeración en los contenedores de Maersk Sealand.

El EMD F40PH ha seguido prestando servicio a VIA Rail en el siglo XXI: entre 2007 y 2012, VIA renovó toda su flota por 100 millones de dólares canadienses. El programa de reconstrucción incluyó generadores HEP separados, motores reacondicionados, la adición de un tercer faro, reacondicionamiento de la cabina, bocinas de seguridad adicionales en la parte delantera y repintado según el nuevo esquema VIA. La locomotora reconstruida n.° 6403, que arrastra al _canadiense_ a través de las Montañas Rocosas, se incluyó en el reverso del billete de diez dólares canadiense rediseñado en 2013 (el 6403 real pasó a ser más tarde 6459). A partir de 2018 VIA tiene en servicio 53 locomotoras EMD F40PH de este tipo. Estas locomotoras F40PH se complementan ahora con las locomotoras GE P42DC entregadas en 2001 y con las locomotoras Siemens SCV-42 entregadas en 2023.

Se han conservado tres antiguos F40PH de Amtrak: el número 231 es propiedad de Dynamic Rail Preservation en Boulder City, Nevada, el número 281 está en el Museo del Ferrocarril del Estado de California y el número 307 está en el Museo del Transporte de Carolina del Norte. Coaster donó dos de sus locomotoras F40PHM-2C que fueron retiradas el 8 de febrero de 2021; El 2103 fue donado al Museo del Ferrocarril del Suroeste del Pacífico y el 2105 al Museo del Ferrocarril del Sur de California.

Variantes
---------

[![Image 5: Rust-red locomotive with smooth front in rail yard](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Speno_International_RMS101_at_CP_Yard_at_Coquitlam%2C_BC_on_September_20%2C_1987_%2822423087108%29.jpg/220px-Speno_International_RMS101_at_CP_Yard_at_Coquitlam%2C_BC_on_September_20%2C_1987_%2822423087108%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Speno_International_RMS101_at_CP_Yard_at_Coquitlam,_BC_on_September_20,_1987_(22423087108).jpg)

Speno EMD F40PH-2M No. 101 en Coquitlam, Columbia Británica en 1987

[![Image 6: White and blue locomotive](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/AMTK_90225_Caltrain927.jpg/220px-AMTK_90225_Caltrain927.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AMTK_90225_Caltrain927.jpg)

Amtrak NPCU No. 90225 en el _San Joaquin_ en Martínez en noviembre de 2013

La longevidad del F40PH ha dado lugar a numerosas conversiones, reconstrucciones y refabricaciones. En algunos casos, se ensamblaron locomotoras nuevas utilizando componentes EMD. Varias agencias de transporte alargaron sus locomotoras para incluir un generador HEP independiente. Estos fueron designados **F40PH-2C** y **F40PH-CAT** donde se utilizaron generadores Cummins y Caterpillar, respectivamente. El F40PH-2C era considerablemente más pesado que el diseño estándar, con un peso de 282 000 lb (128 000 kg). El **F40PH-2D**, empleado por Via Rail, tenía personalizaciones especiales para operar en Canadá, incluidas luces de zanjas. Las últimas 30 locomotoras de Metra, denominadas **F40PHM-2** (ahora reconstruidas como **F40PHM-3**), se construyeron con una cabina inclinada similar a la EMD F69PHAC experimental. Su aspecto estilizado recibió el sobrenombre de "Winnebago". Las cuatro locomotoras de Speno, denominadas **F40PH-2M**, se entregaron sin turbocompresores, lo que limitaba la potencia de salida a 2000 caballos de fuerza (1500 kW). Las cinco locomotoras EMD GP40 que Morrison-Knudsen reconstruyó para Tri-Rail en 1988 fueron designadas **F40PHL-2**. Progress Rail reconstruyó 41 unidades Metra con motores remanufacturados, motores de tracción reconstruidos y control de tracción por microprocesador. Estos han sido designados **F40PH-3**. La docena de locomotoras **F40PHM-2C** de MBTA se construyeron nuevas utilizando componentes EMD, al igual que las seis locomotoras **F40PH-3** del Altamont Commuter Express.

A medida que la flota F40PH de Amtrak fue reemplazada por locomotoras más nuevas de la serie GE Genesis, Amtrak convirtió varias de las unidades retiradas en vagones de equipaje/taxi. Conocidas coloquialmente como "coles" (un acrónimo de "taxi" y "equipaje"), y oficialmente conocidas como **Unidades de control no motorizadas** (NPCU), estas unidades tenían sus motores diésel, Se quitaron los motores de tracción y los alternadores principales, así como una gran puerta enrollable instalada en el lateral (que permite utilizar el antiguo compartimento del motor para el equipaje). Amtrak convirtió 22 locomotoras en vagones repollo entre 1996 y 2007. Cada unidad convertida pasó a numerarse con el prefijo "90" a su número original. En 2011, Amtrak convirtió el F40PH No. 406 en una NPCU para permitir la operación push-pull del tren de exhibición del 40 aniversario de Amtrak; además, se instaló un generador HEP para suministrar energía auxiliar. A diferencia de otras NPCU, el No. 406 conserva su número original (en lugar de ser renumerado a 90406) y externamente se parece a un F40PH operativo.

Algunos F40PH llegaron al servicio de transporte de mercancías, después de las modificaciones adecuadas. El **F40M-2F**, que circula por el Ferrocarril de San Luis y Río Grande y anteriormente el Ferrocarril Americano Canadiense, fue ajustado para una velocidad máxima de 65 millas por hora (105 km/h) y se le dio un tamaño ampliado. Tanque de combustible de 2900 galones estadounidenses (11 000 l; 2400 imp gal). También estaba equipado con puerta, plataforma y escalones en la parte delantera. Una unidad, 450, fue adquirida por Western Maryland Scenic Railroad en 2018.

Propietarios originales
-----------------------

La División Electro-Motive fabricó 475 F40PH de todo tipo entre 1975 y 1992. Los pedidos de GO Transit y VIA Rail Canada fueron realizados por General Motors Diesel (GMD), la filial canadiense de la empresa. Morrison-Knudsen y su sucesora MotivePower remanufacturaron otras 31 locomotoras entre 1988 y 1998.
